items.explanation: Marshall's 1803 ruling struck down part of the Judiciary Act of 1789, establishing that the Supreme Court may void acts of Congress that violate the Constitution.
options: A. Expanded presidential powers claimed by Jefferson's Republicans
B. Gave broad new powers to state courts
C. Upheld the Alien and Sedition Acts
D. Established the principle of judicial review

option_explanations.A: Marbury did not expand Jefferson's presidential power. Marshall's ruling asserted the judiciary's power to overrule the other branches — a check on the president, not an enlargement of him.
option_explanations.B: Marbury gave no new powers to state courts. It established the power of the federal Supreme Court to void acts of Congress.
option_explanations.C: Marbury did not uphold the Alien and Sedition Acts. The Sedition Act had already expired in 1801, and the case concerned judicial appointments, not those laws.
option_explanations.D: Correct. In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Marshall struck down part of the Judiciary Act of 1789, establishing judicial review — the Supreme Court's power to void acts of Congress that violate the Constitution.

items.explanation: Jefferson's 'Revolution of 1800' cut the federal establishment: he repealed internal excise taxes (including the whiskey tax), shrank the army, and attacked the national debt.
options: A. Increased aid to the commercial sector
B. Made foreign policy more pro-British
C. Drove the federal debt sharply upward
D. Eliminated federal excise taxes
items.stem: As a result of Jefferson's election in 1800,

option_explanations.A: Jefferson did not increase aid to the commercial sector. His 'Revolution of 1800' favored agrarian interests and cut the Federalist-era supports for commerce and finance.
option_explanations.B: Jefferson's foreign policy was not pro-British. He leaned toward France early on, and his Embargo of 1807 damaged trade with both Britain and France.
option_explanations.C: Jefferson did not drive the debt upward. Under Gallatin's management he attacked the national debt and shrank the army and the federal establishment.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Jefferson's 'Revolution of 1800' repealed the federal internal excise taxes — including the whiskey tax that had sparked rebellion — and cut the federal establishment.

items.explanation: America went to war over impressment, British aid to western tribes, and War Hawk hunger for Canada and Florida — but with an army of 6,000 men and 17 ships, no one claimed the navy was ready to show its strength.
options: A. The impressment of American sailors
B. A powerful American navy eager to prove itself
C. British support for western Native tribes
D. American designs on Canada and Florida
items.stem: All of the following help explain why America entered the War of 1812 EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Impressment of American sailors was a real cause: British warships stopped American vessels and seized sailors, an insult the War Hawks would not tolerate.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the exception. America had no powerful navy eager to prove itself: the regular army numbered about 6,000 men and the navy had roughly 17 ships, so naval ambition did not drive the war.
option_explanations.C: British support for western Native tribes was a real cause: Westerners blamed Britain for arming Tecumseh's confederacy and other resisting tribes.
option_explanations.D: American designs on Canada and Florida were a real cause: War Hawks like Clay and Calhoun openly coveted Canada and Spanish Florida.

items.explanation: New England Federalists at Hartford in 1814 discussed nullifying federal war measures — proving that nullification talk was a sectional tactic, not a Southern invention.
options: A. The Federalist Party remained nationally dominant
B. The War of 1812 unified American politics
C. Nullification was not an exclusively Southern doctrine
D. The Treaty of Ghent deeply divided the country

option_explanations.A: The Federalist Party was not nationally dominant in 1814; it was dying. The Hartford Convention hastened its demise by tarring Federalists as disloyal.
option_explanations.B: The War of 1812 did not unify American politics. Federalist opposition to 'Mr. Madison's War' — culminating in the Hartford Convention — showed how divided the country was.
option_explanations.C: Correct. New England Federalists at Hartford in 1814 discussed nullifying federal war measures — proving that nullification was a sectional tactic available to any region, not a Southern invention.
option_explanations.D: The Treaty of Ghent (1814) ended the war; it was not what divided the country. The Convention's grievance was the war itself and Republican war measures.

items.explanation: Clay's program — a national bank, protective tariffs, and federally funded internal improvements — aimed to build a self-sufficient American economy.
options: A. Promoted economic growth, a national bank, and protective tariffs
B. Sought military parity with Britain and France
C. Favored lower tariffs to encourage imports
D. Called for the abolition of slavery

option_explanations.A: Correct. Clay's American System promoted a national bank, protective tariffs, and federally funded internal improvements — a program to build a self-sufficient, growing American economy.
option_explanations.B: The American System was an economic program, not a military one; it said nothing about matching Britain's or France's armed forces.
option_explanations.C: Clay favored higher protective tariffs to shield American manufacturers, not lower tariffs to encourage imports — the opposite of this option.
option_explanations.D: The American System said nothing about abolishing slavery. Clay was himself a slaveholder; his program was about banking, tariffs, and roads and canals.

items.explanation: Tecumseh tells Harrison the tribes must 'unite, and let them consider their lands as the common property of the whole' -- land belonging to all Native peoples together, so no single chief could sell it. He rejects both individual tribal ownership and sale to the highest bidder, and the British crown owned nothing here.
options: A. Land belonged to all Native peoples in common, so no chief could sell it
B. Each tribe owned its own territory absolutely
C. Tribal land should be sold to the highest bidder
D. The British crown held title to all Native land
items.stem: According to the passage, Tecumseh's view of Native land ownership was that
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"Brother, since the peace was made, you have killed some of the Shawnees, Winnebagoes, Delawares, and Miamis, and you have taken our land from us... The way, and the only way, to check and to stop this evil, is for all the red men to unite in claiming a common and equal right in the land."
—Tecumseh to William Henry Harrison, 1810 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Tecumseh tells Harrison that the tribes must 'unite in claiming a common and equal right in the land' — land belonging to all Native peoples together, so that no single chief could sell it away.
option_explanations.B: Tecumseh rejects the idea that each tribe owned its territory absolutely. That view is what let Americans buy land piecemeal from individual chiefs — the very practice he is condemning.
option_explanations.C: Tecumseh opposes selling tribal land entirely, let alone auctioning it to the highest bidder. His whole argument is against the sale of Native land.
option_explanations.D: The British crown held no title to Native land in this argument. Tecumseh's claim is that the land belongs to the Native peoples in common, not to any European monarch.

items.explanation: Tecumseh accuses Harrison: 'you take tribes aside and advise them not to come into this measure' -- the American practice of buying land from individual chiefs (as at the Treaty of Fort Wayne, 1809) to fracture the united front Tecumseh was building. It was divide-and-rule through separate treaties.
options: A. Offering United States citizenship to Native peoples
B. Building mission schools for Native children
C. Negotiating land cessions with individual chiefs to break Native unity
D. Banning all trade between settlers and Native peoples
items.stem: The American tactic Tecumseh condemns in the passage was
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"Brother, since the peace was made, you have killed some of the Shawnees, Winnebagoes, Delawares, and Miamis, and you have taken our land from us... The way, and the only way, to check and to stop this evil, is for all the red men to unite in claiming a common and equal right in the land."
—Tecumseh to William Henry Harrison, 1810 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The United States was not offering Native peoples citizenship in this period; citizenship for Native Americans came far later. This was not the tactic Tecumseh condemns.
option_explanations.B: Mission schools were not the tactic at issue. Tecumseh's complaint is about land negotiations, not education.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Tecumseh accuses Harrison of taking 'tribes aside' — the American practice of negotiating land cessions with individual chiefs, as at the Treaty of Fort Wayne (1809), to break the united front Tecumseh was building.
option_explanations.D: The United States was not banning trade with Native peoples; traders were in fact the advance agents of American expansion. The condemned tactic was divide-and-rule through separate treaties.

items.explanation: Tecumseh's confederacy needed what only Britain could provide: muskets, powder, and a great-power counterweight to the United States. The alliance was strategic, not cultural -- at the Thames in 1813 Tecumseh died fighting alongside the British, and with him the confederacy died too.
options: A. Tecumseh hoped to make his people British subjects
B. Only Britain could supply the arms and diplomatic backing needed to resist the United States
C. France had refused to provide any assistance
D. Harrison had advised him to seek British aid
items.stem: Tecumseh's confederacy sought an alliance with Britain during the War of 1812 primarily because
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"Brother, since the peace was made, you have killed some of the Shawnees, Winnebagoes, Delawares, and Miamis, and you have taken our land from us... The way, and the only way, to check and to stop this evil, is for all the red men to unite in claiming a common and equal right in the land."
—Tecumseh to William Henry Harrison, 1810 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Tecumseh did not want his people to become British subjects. The alliance was strategic — arms and backing for resistance — not a bid for subjecthood.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Tecumseh's confederacy needed what only Britain could provide: muskets, powder, and a great-power counterweight to the United States. At the Thames in 1813 he died fighting alongside the British, and the confederacy died with him.
option_explanations.C: France was not a factor: it had sold Louisiana in 1803 and was consumed by the Napoleonic wars. There was no French assistance to refuse.
option_explanations.D: Harrison was Tecumseh's enemy, not his adviser. He would never have advised Tecumseh to seek British aid; he was the one Tecumseh was resisting.
